subject: Anatomy
title: Lower Limb

source.book: Recall by Yanal — Upper & Lower Limb Anatomy
source.title: Lower Limb

objectives: Identify the key structures of Lower Limb at each level of dissection.
Relate the nerves, vessels and muscles of Lower Limb to their functions.
Localise the named spaces and regions of Lower Limb and list their contents.
Recognise the common clinical lesions associated with Lower Limb.
Reproduce the high-yield relations of Lower Limb tested in vivas and MCQs.

glossary.def: L2-L4 nerve of the anterior thigh; supplies quadriceps and skin via the saphenous nerve.
Largest nerve in the body (L4-S3); divides into tibial and common fibular nerves.
Larger terminal branch of the sciatic supplying the posterior leg and sole.
Sciatic branch winding round the fibular neck; injury causes foot drop.
L2-L4 nerve to the medial (adductor) compartment of the thigh.
L4-S1 nerve to gluteus medius/minimus; injury gives a Trendelenburg gait.
Region bounded by inguinal ligament, sartorius and adductor longus; contents NAVEL.
Medial compartment of the femoral sheath; site of femoral hernia.
Aponeurotic tunnel transmitting the femoral vessels and saphenous nerve to the popliteal fossa.
Diamond behind the knee containing the popliteal vessels and tibial/common fibular nerves.
Space behind the medial malleolus deep to the flexor retinaculum (Tom, Dick, ANd Harry).
Longest vein of the body; ascends medially to the saphenofemoral junction.
Continuation of the external iliac artery in the thigh; becomes popliteal at the adductor hiatus.
Dorsal foot pulse lateral to the EHL tendon; assesses distal perfusion.
Rectus femoris and three vasti; the knee extensor, femoral-innervated.
Biceps femoris, semitendinosus and semimembranosus; hip extensors and knee flexors.
Hip abductor stabilising the pelvis in single-leg stance.
Loss of ankle dorsiflexion from common-fibular-nerve palsy, giving a high-stepping gait.
Pelvic drop on the swing side from weak hip abductors (superior gluteal nerve).
Bowel protruding through the femoral canal below and lateral to the pubic tubercle; often irreducible.
Combined injury of ACL, MCL and medial meniscus from a lateral blow to the flexed knee.
Calf pain on walking relieved by rest, from peripheral arterial disease.
Thick central fascia of the sole supporting the longitudinal arch.
Group of muscles supplied by a single spinal nerve root.

mnemonics.expansion: Femoral triangle, lateral to medial: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space, Lymphatics
Behind the medial malleolus: Tibialis posterior, flexor Digitorum longus, posterior tibial Artery, tibial Nerve, flexor Hallucis longus

Iliotibial tract and the gluteal tuberosity of the femur
Inferior gluteal nerve (L5–S2)

External ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines
Lateral surface of the greater trochanter
Superior gluteal nerve (L4–S1)
Abducts and medially rotates the thigh; steadies the pelvis during the stance phase of gait (its loss gives a Trendelenburg sign)
External ilium between the anterior and inferior gluteal lines
Anterior surface of the greater trochanter
Superior gluteal nerve (L4–S1)
Abducts and medially rotates the thigh; a pelvic stabiliser with gluteus medius
Anterior superior iliac spine and anterior iliac crest
Iliotibial tract (which inserts on the lateral tibial condyle, Gerdy's tubercle)
Superior gluteal nerve (L4–S1)

Anterior surface of the sacrum
Superior border of the greater trochanter
Nerve to piriformis (ventral rami) (S1–S2)
Laterally rotates the extended thigh and abducts the flexed thigh; the key landmark of the gluteal region (nerves exit above and below it)
Internal surface of the obturator membrane and surrounding bone
Medial surface of the greater trochanter (trochanteric fossa region)
Nerve to obturator internus (L5–S1)
Laterally rotates the extended thigh and abducts the flexed thigh
Lateral border of the ischial tuberosity
Quadrate tubercle on the intertrochanteric crest of the femur
Nerve to quadratus femoris (L5–S1)
Laterally rotates the thigh and steadies the femoral head in the acetabulum
External surface of the obturator membrane and margins of the obturator foramen
Trochanteric fossa of the femur
Obturator nerve (L3–L4)
Laterally rotates the thigh and stabilises the femoral head
Transverse processes, bodies and discs of T12–L5
Lesser trochanter of the femur (as iliopsoas)
Anterior rami of L1–L3 (L1–L3)
Chief flexor of the thigh at the hip (and flexes the trunk); a psoas abscess can track along it to the thigh
Iliac fossa and ala of the sacrum
Lesser trochanter of the femur (with psoas, as iliopsoas)
Femoral nerve (L2–L3)
Flexes the thigh at the hip and stabilises the hip joint
Anterior superior iliac spine
Superomedial tibia at the pes anserinus
Femoral nerve (L2–L3)
Flexes, abducts and laterally rotates the thigh and flexes the knee ('tailor's position'); the longest muscle in the body
Anterior inferior iliac spine and the rim of the acetabulum
Base of the patella, then the tibial tuberosity via the patellar ligament
Femoral nerve (L2–L4)
Extends the knee and flexes the hip (the only quadriceps head crossing the hip joint)
Greater trochanter and lateral lip of the linea aspera
Patella then tibial tuberosity via the quadriceps/patellar tendon
Femoral nerve (L2–L4)
Extends the knee; the usual site for intramuscular injection in the thigh
Intertrochanteric line and medial lip of the linea aspera
Patella then tibial tuberosity via the quadriceps/patellar tendon
Femoral nerve (L2–L4)
Extends the knee; its oblique fibres (VMO) stabilise the patella against lateral dislocation
Anterior and lateral surfaces of the femoral shaft
Patella then tibial tuberosity via the quadriceps/patellar tendon
Femoral nerve (L2–L4)
Extends the knee
Pecten pubis (superior pubic ramus)
Pectineal line of the femur (below the lesser trochanter)
Femoral nerve (occasionally also obturator) (L2–L3)
Adducts and flexes the thigh; forms part of the floor of the femoral triangle
Body of the pubis below the pubic crest
Middle third of the linea aspera
Obturator nerve (anterior division) (L2–L4)
Adducts the thigh; its medial border helps bound the femoral triangle
Body and inferior ramus of the pubis
Pectineal line and proximal linea aspera
Obturator nerve (L2–L4)
Adducts the thigh (the anterior and posterior divisions of the obturator nerve straddle it)
Adductor part: ischiopubic ramus; hamstring part: ischial tuberosity
Linea aspera, medial supracondylar line and the adductor tubercle
Adductor part: obturator nerve; hamstring part: tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L2–L4)
Powerful adductor (adductor part) and extensor (hamstring part) of the thigh; the adductor hiatus in its tendon transmits the femoral vessels to the popliteal fossa
Body and inferior ramus of the pubis
Superomedial tibia at the pes anserinus
Obturator nerve (L2–L3)
Adducts the thigh and flexes the knee; the only medial-compartment muscle to cross the knee (used for tendon/muscle grafts)
Long head: ischial tuberosity; Short head: linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line
Head of the fibula
Long head: tibial division; Short head: common fibular division of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2)
Flexes the knee and laterally rotates the flexed leg; the long head extends the hip
Ischial tuberosity
Superomedial tibia at the pes anserinus
Tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2)
Extends the hip, flexes the knee and medially rotates the flexed leg
Ischial tuberosity
Posterior part of the medial tibial condyle
Tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2)
Extends the hip, flexes the knee and medially rotates the flexed leg
Lateral tibial condyle, upper lateral tibia and interosseous membrane
Medial cuneiform and base of the 1st metatarsal
Deep fibular nerve (L4–L5)
Dorsiflexes the ankle and inverts the foot; its loss causes foot drop
Middle fibula and interosseous membrane
Base of the distal phalanx of the great toe
Deep fibular nerve (L5–S1)
Extends the great toe and helps dorsiflex the ankle
Lateral tibial condyle, anterior fibula and interosseous membrane
Extensor expansions of the lateral four toes
Deep fibular nerve (L5–S1)
Extends the toes and dorsiflexes the ankle
Distal anterior fibula and interosseous membrane
Base of the 5th metatarsal
Deep fibular nerve (L5–S1)
Dorsiflexes the ankle and everts the foot (a partly separated part of extensor digitorum longus)
Head and upper lateral surface of the fibula
Medial cuneiform and base of the 1st metatarsal (crossing the sole)
Superficial fibular nerve (L5–S1)
Everts and plantarflexes the foot and supports the transverse and lateral longitudinal arches
Lower lateral surface of the fibula
Tuberosity of the 5th metatarsal
Superficial fibular nerve (L5–S1)
Everts and plantarflexes the foot (avulsion of its insertion causes a base-of-5th-metatarsal fracture)
Lateral and medial condyles of the femur
Calcaneus via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon
Tibial nerve (S1–S2)
Plantarflexes the ankle and flexes the knee; the main propulsive calf muscle
Soleal line and posterior tibia, and the head/posterior fibula
Calcaneus via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon
Tibial nerve (S1–S2)
Plantarflexes the ankle; a postural muscle and the chief 'calf pump' returning venous blood
Lateral supracondylar line of the femur
Calcaneus (medial to the calcaneal tendon)
Tibial nerve (S1–S2)
Weakly plantarflexes the ankle and flexes the knee (a long slender tendon, often harvested for grafts)
Lateral condyle of the femur and the lateral meniscus
Posterior tibia above the soleal line
Tibial nerve (L4–S1)
'Unlocks' the extended knee by laterally rotating the femur on the fixed tibia to begin flexion
Posterior surface of the fibula and interosseous membrane
Base of the distal phalanx of the great toe
Tibial nerve (S1–S2)
Flexes the great toe and plantarflexes the ankle; supports the medial longitudinal arch during push-off
Medial posterior surface of the tibia
Bases of the distal phalanges of the lateral four toes
Tibial nerve (S1–S2)
Flexes the lateral four toes and plantarflexes/inverts the foot
Posterior tibia, fibula and interosseous membrane
Navicular tuberosity, cuneiforms and bases of the 2nd–4th metatarsals
Tibial nerve (L4–L5)
Chief invertor of the foot and a plantarflexor; the key dynamic support of the medial longitudinal arch
Dorsal surface of the calcaneus
Extensor expansions/proximal phalanges of the medial four toes (its medial slip = extensor hallucis brevis)
Deep fibular nerve (S1–S2)
Aids extension of the toes; forms the soft fleshy bulge on the lateral dorsum of the foot
Medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity
Medial base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe
Medial plantar nerve (S1–S2)
Abducts and flexes the great toe; a first-layer sole muscle supporting the medial arch
Medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity and plantar aponeurosis
Middle phalanges of the lateral four toes
Medial plantar nerve (S1–S2)
Flexes the lateral four toes (first sole layer, analogous to FDS in the hand)
Medial and lateral margins of the plantar calcaneus
Tendon of flexor digitorum longus
Lateral plantar nerve (S1–S3)
Straightens the oblique pull of flexor digitorum longus so the toes flex directly (second sole layer)
Oblique head: bases of metatarsals 2–4; Transverse head: MTP ligaments of lateral toes
Lateral base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe
Deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3)
Adducts the great toe and helps maintain the transverse arch (third sole layer)
Metatarsal shafts (plantar unipennate; dorsal bipennate)
Proximal phalanges/extensor expansions
Lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3)
Plantar interossei ADduct the toes (PAD) toward the 2nd toe; dorsal interossei ABduct (DAB) — reference axis is the 2nd toe

cards.front: Femoral nerve — root value and origin?
cards.back: L2, L3, L4 — the largest branch of the lumbar plexus (posterior divisions)

cards.front: Femoral nerve — how does it enter the thigh?
cards.back: Behind the inguinal ligament, LATERAL to the femoral artery and femoral sheath (so it is outside the sheath)
The anterior thigh: iliacus, pectineus, sartorius and the quadriceps femoris (knee extensors)
Anterior thigh; its saphenous branch supplies the medial leg and medial foot
Weak/absent knee extension (buckling knee), lost patellar reflex and sensory loss over the anterior thigh and medial leg
L2, L3, L4 (anterior divisions of the lumbar plexus)

cards.front: Obturator nerve — where does it enter the thigh?
cards.back: Through the obturator foramen into the medial compartment
The adductor muscles: adductor longus, brevis, magnus (adductor part), gracilis and obturator externus

cards.front: Obturator nerve — sensory supply and referred pain?
cards.back: Skin of the medial thigh; hip pathology can refer pain to the medial thigh/knee via this nerve

cards.front: Sciatic nerve — root value and origin?
cards.back: L4–S3 — the largest nerve in the body, from the sacral plexus

cards.front: Sciatic nerve — how does it leave the pelvis?
cards.back: Through the greater sciatic foramen, usually BELOW piriformis
The tibial and common fibular (peroneal) divisions, bound together until they separate at the apex of the popliteal fossa

cards.front: Sciatic nerve — muscles supplied in the thigh?
cards.back: The hamstrings and the hamstring part of adductor magnus (no motor supply to muscles above the knee otherwise)

cards.front: Sciatic nerve — classic causes of injury?
cards.back: Posterior hip dislocation and a badly placed intramuscular injection (hence injecting into the upper outer quadrant)
The larger terminal division of the sciatic nerve; runs down the popliteal fossa and posterior leg, then behind the medial malleolus
The posterior compartment of the leg (calf) and, via the medial and lateral plantar nerves, the sole of the foot

cards.front: Tibial nerve — where is it vulnerable at the ankle?
cards.back: In the tarsal tunnel behind the medial malleolus (tarsal tunnel syndrome)

cards.front: Tibial nerve — effect of a proximal injury?
cards.back: Loss of plantarflexion and toe flexion, a calcaneovalgus foot and loss of sole sensation (cannot stand on tiptoe)

cards.front: Common fibular (peroneal) nerve — origin and vulnerable point?
cards.back: The smaller terminal division of the sciatic nerve; winds superficially around the neck of the fibula — the MOST commonly injured nerve in the lower limb

cards.front: Common fibular nerve — its two branches?
cards.back: Superficial fibular (lateral compartment + dorsum sensation) and deep fibular (anterior compartment + first web space)
The anterior compartment (dorsiflexors) and skin of the first web space; its loss is central to foot drop
Fibularis longus and brevis (evertors) and the skin over most of the dorsum of the foot
Foot drop with a high-stepping gait, and loss of eversion and dorsiflexion (equinovarus tendency)

cards.front: Superior gluteal nerve — root value and course?
cards.back: L4–S1; leaves the pelvis ABOVE piriformis through the greater sciatic foramen
Gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae
A positive Trendelenburg sign — the pelvis drops on the UNsupported (contralateral) side when standing on the affected leg

cards.front: Inferior gluteal nerve — root value and course?
cards.back: L5–S2; leaves the pelvis BELOW piriformis
Gluteus maximus (so injury impairs rising from sitting, climbing stairs and jumping)

cards.front: Lumbar plexus — root value and where it lies?
cards.back: T12–L4, formed within the substance of psoas major
Iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, genitofemoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, femoral and obturator nerves
L4–S4 (the lumbosacral trunk, L4–L5, links the lumbar and sacral plexuses)
Superior and inferior gluteal nerves, the sciatic nerve, the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve and the pudendal nerve

cards.front: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve — clinical syndrome?
cards.back: Its entrapment under the inguinal ligament causes meralgia paraesthetica (burning numbness over the lateral thigh)

cards.front: Which nerve roots contribute to the sciatic nerve?
cards.back: L4, L5, S1, S2 and S3
Ilium, ischium and pubis, which fuse at the acetabulum (at the triradiate cartilage)

cards.front: Hip bone — landmarks for surface anatomy?
cards.back: ASIS and PSIS, iliac crest, pubic tubercle and ischial tuberosity are key palpable landmarks

cards.front: Hip bone — greater & lesser sciatic notches?
cards.back: Converted into foramina by the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments; the ischial spine separates them
The cup for the femoral head; its non-articular floor is the acetabular fossa and the rim is deepened by the acetabular labrum

cards.front: Femur — head and its blood supply?
cards.back: Articulates with the acetabulum; supplied mainly by retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery, with a small contribution from the artery of ligamentum teres
Common fracture site in the elderly; an intracapsular fracture may disrupt the retinacular vessels and cause avascular necrosis of the head
Greater trochanter: gluteus medius/minimus and lateral rotators; lesser trochanter: iliopsoas
The line (anterior) gives attachment to the iliofemoral ligament; the crest (posterior) bears the quadrate tubercle
A rough posterior ridge for the adductors, vastus muscles and short head of biceps femoris
On the medial condyle; insertion of the hamstring part of adductor magnus (a guide to the adductor hiatus)
Medial and lateral condyles articulate with the tibia; the anterior patellar surface (trochlea) articulates with the patella
The largest sesamoid bone, lying within the quadriceps tendon; it improves the leverage of knee extension
The medial, weight-bearing bone of the leg; its subcutaneous anterior border and medial surface form the 'shin'
Medial and lateral condyles bear the menisci; the intercondylar eminence anchors the cruciate ligaments and menisci
Anterior prominence for the patellar ligament (site of Osgood–Schlatter disease in adolescents)
Distal medial projection forming the medial wall of the ankle mortise; the deltoid ligament attaches here
Bears little weight; provides muscle attachment and forms the lateral malleolus (lateral wall of the ankle mortise)
The common fibular nerve winds around the neck and is easily injured by fractures or a tight plaster cast
Talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid and three cuneiforms (medial, intermediate, lateral)
Transmits body weight to the foot, has NO muscle attachments, and its retrograde blood supply risks avascular necrosis after fracture
The largest tarsal bone (the heel); the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon inserts on its tuberosity and the sustentaculum tali supports the talus
Insertion of fibularis brevis; a common avulsion-fracture site (distinguish from a Jones fracture of the base)
Medial longitudinal (highest), lateral longitudinal and transverse arches distribute weight and act as shock absorbers

cards.front: Foot — supports of the medial arch?
cards.back: Bone shape, the spring (plantar calcaneonavicular) ligament, plantar aponeurosis and tibialis posterior/flexor tendons
A ball-and-socket synovial joint; very stable (deep acetabulum + labrum + strong ligaments) yet allows a wide range of movement
The iliofemoral ligament (the inverted-Y of Bigelow), which limits hyperextension and helps you stand upright

cards.front: Hip joint — the three capsular ligaments?
cards.back: Iliofemoral, pubofemoral and ischiofemoral ligaments (they spiral and tighten in extension)
The limb is shortened, adducted and medially rotated, and the sciatic nerve is at risk
The largest synovial joint; a modified hinge allowing flexion/extension and slight rotation when flexed
The ACL prevents anterior displacement of the tibia (torn in the 'unhappy triad'); the PCL prevents posterior displacement
The medial (tibial) collateral is attached to the medial meniscus (so both tear together); the lateral (fibular) collateral is cord-like and separate from its meniscus
Fibrocartilage pads that deepen the tibial surface, absorb shock and aid load distribution; the medial meniscus is more often torn
The knee 'locks' by medial rotation of the femur in full extension; popliteus 'unlocks' it to begin flexion
A lateral blow tears the ACL, the medial collateral ligament and the medial meniscus together
A hinge synovial joint; the tibia and fibula form a mortise gripping the talus (most stable in dorsiflexion, when the wider talus is wedged in)

cards.front: Ankle joint — medial vs lateral ligaments?
cards.back: The medial (deltoid) ligament is strong and rarely torn; the lateral ligaments are weaker — the anterior talofibular ligament is the most commonly sprained
Inversion of the plantarflexed foot, tearing the anterior talofibular ligament
Superior: a plane synovial joint; inferior: a fibrous syndesmosis that keeps the ankle mortise tight
Inversion and eversion of the foot (with the transverse tarsal joint)
Superiorly the inguinal ligament, laterally sartorius, medially the medial border of adductor longus; floor = iliopsoas + pectineus; roof = fascia lata

cards.front: Femoral triangle — contents lateral to medial (NAVEL)?
cards.back: Femoral Nerve, femoral Artery, femoral Vein, Empty space (femoral canal), Lymphatics

cards.front: Femoral triangle — surface landmark for the femoral artery?
cards.back: The mid-inguinal point (midway between the ASIS and the pubic symphysis) — the site to feel the femoral pulse and for arterial access

cards.front: Femoral sheath — what does it contain (and not)?
cards.back: A funnel of transversalis/iliac fascia enclosing the femoral artery, femoral vein and femoral canal — but NOT the femoral nerve (which lies lateral to it)
The medial compartment of the sheath; contains fat and the lymph node of Cloquet, and allows the vein to expand; its upper opening is the femoral ring

cards.front: Femoral hernia — where does it appear?
cards.back: Below and lateral to the pubic tubercle (through the femoral canal); commoner in females and prone to strangulation because of the narrow, rigid ring

cards.front: Femoral vs inguinal hernia — the key landmark?
cards.back: Relative to the pubic tubercle: an inguinal hernia is above and medial, a femoral hernia is below and lateral

cards.front: Adductor (subsartorial / Hunter's) canal — what does it transmit?
cards.back: The femoral artery, femoral vein, the saphenous nerve and the nerve to vastus medialis
Bounded by vastus medialis, the adductors and the sartorius roof; it ends at the adductor hiatus, where the vessels pass to the popliteal fossa
Superolaterally biceps femoris, superomedially semimembranosus/semitendinosus, and inferiorly the two heads of gastrocnemius

cards.front: Popliteal fossa — contents from deep to superficial?
cards.back: Popliteal artery (deepest), popliteal vein, then the tibial nerve; the common fibular nerve runs along the lateral (biceps) margin
The commonest site of peripheral arterial aneurysm; a Baker's (popliteal) cyst can present here

cards.front: Gluteal region — the key landmark muscle?
cards.back: Piriformis — structures emerge above it (superior gluteal nerve/vessels) or below it (inferior gluteal nerve, sciatic nerve, pudendal nerve, posterior femoral cutaneous nerve)

cards.front: Gluteal region — safe site for intramuscular injection?
cards.back: The upper outer (superolateral) quadrant, to avoid the sciatic nerve and gluteal vessels

cards.front: Gluteal region — structures passing through the LESSER sciatic foramen?
cards.back: The tendon of obturator internus, the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels (which re-enter the perineum)
Anterior (dorsiflexors, deep fibular nerve), lateral (evertors, superficial fibular nerve), superficial posterior (gastrocnemius/soleus) and deep posterior (deep flexors, tibial nerve)
The commonest leg compartment syndrome; raised pressure compresses the anterior tibial vessels and deep fibular nerve — pain on passive stretch and first-web-space numbness; treated by fasciotomy

cards.front: Leg compartments — the '5 Ps' of compartment syndrome?
cards.back: Pain (out of proportion, on passive stretch), Paraesthesia, Pallor, Pulselessness (late) and Paralysis (late)
Behind and below the medial malleolus, roofed by the flexor retinaculum

cards.front: Tarsal tunnel — contents (Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry)?
cards.back: Tibialis posterior, flexor Digitorum longus, posterior tibial Artery, posterior tibial Vein, tibial Nerve, flexor Hallucis longus

cards.front: Plantar aponeurosis — role and clinical lesion?
cards.back: A thick central band from the calcaneus supporting the medial longitudinal arch; inflammation causes plantar fasciitis (heel pain worst on the first steps)
Continues the external iliac artery behind the inguinal ligament at the mid-inguinal point
The profunda femoris (deep artery of the thigh), which gives the medial and lateral circumflex femoral and the perforating arteries

cards.front: Femoral artery — which vessel supplies most of the femoral head?
cards.back: The medial circumflex femoral artery (via retinacular branches)

cards.front: Femoral artery — where does it become the popliteal artery?
cards.back: At the adductor hiatus (the opening in adductor magnus)

cards.front: Popliteal artery — course and terminal branches?
cards.back: The deepest structure in the popliteal fossa; it divides at the lower border of popliteus into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries
Supply the knee and form an anastomosis around the joint (important collateral circulation)

cards.front: Anterior tibial artery — course and continuation?
cards.back: Descends in the anterior compartment on the interosseous membrane and continues onto the dorsum of the foot as the dorsalis pedis artery

cards.front: Dorsalis pedis pulse — where is it felt?
cards.back: On the dorsum of the foot, lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus

cards.front: Posterior tibial artery — course and pulse?
cards.back: Descends in the deep posterior compartment and passes behind the medial malleolus (its pulse point) into the sole as the medial and lateral plantar arteries
A branch of the posterior tibial artery supplying the lateral and posterior compartments

The longest vein in the body; begins at the medial dorsal venous arch, passes ANTERIOR to the medial malleolus, ascends the medial leg/thigh and ends at the saphenofemoral junction into the femoral vein
The standard vein for a coronary-artery bypass graft and for a venous 'cutdown' at the ankle (constant position anterior to the medial malleolus); the saphenous nerve lies alongside it
Begins behind the LATERAL malleolus, ascends the back of the calf and drains into the popliteal vein

Incompetent valves (often at the saphenofemoral junction or perforators) cause dilated tortuous superficial veins; complications include venous eczema, lipodermatosclerosis and gaiter-area venous ulcers

cards.front: Lower limb — main lymph node group?
cards.back: The superficial and deep inguinal nodes; deep drainage follows the femoral vessels to the external iliac nodes

cards.front: Superficial inguinal nodes — what do they drain?
cards.back: The whole lower limb, the lower anterior abdominal wall, the gluteal region, the perineum and the external genitalia (except the testis/glans specifics)
L2

cards.front: Dermatome — medial side of the knee/leg and medial malleolus?
cards.back: L4

cards.front: Dermatome — dorsum of the foot and great toe web?
cards.back: L5

cards.front: Dermatome — little toe, lateral foot and heel/sole?
cards.back: S1
L1
L3–L4 (femoral nerve)
S1–S2 (tibial nerve)

cards.front: Myotome — dorsiflexion of the great toe (tests which root)?
cards.back: L5 (extensor hallucis longus)
S1–S2

cards.front: Lower-limb lymph — where does the foot/leg ultimately drain?
cards.back: Through the inguinal nodes to the external iliac and para-aortic nodes
Common fibular (peroneal) nerve — loss of dorsiflexion/eversion gives a high-stepping (steppage) gait to clear the toes

cards.front: Common fibular nerve — why is it so often injured?
cards.back: It is subcutaneous as it winds around the neck of the fibula — vulnerable to fractures, tight casts and prolonged leg-crossing
Superior gluteal nerve / gluteus medius weakness — the pelvis DROPS on the unsupported side when standing on the affected leg

cards.front: Sciatic nerve — safe intramuscular injection site?
cards.back: The superolateral (upper outer) quadrant of the buttock, to avoid the sciatic nerve
Weak knee extension (the knee gives way), loss of the patellar reflex and anteromedial sensory loss

cards.front: Tibial nerve injury — deficit and stance?
cards.back: Loss of plantarflexion and toe flexion — the patient cannot stand on tiptoe; sole sensation is lost

cards.front: Tarsal tunnel syndrome — nerve and features?
cards.back: Tibial nerve compression behind the medial malleolus — burning sole pain and paraesthesia

cards.front: Femoral neck fracture — main complication and why?
cards.back: Avascular necrosis of the head, because an intracapsular fracture tears the retinacular vessels (medial circumflex femoral) that supply it

cards.front: Intracapsular vs extracapsular hip fracture — significance?
cards.back: Intracapsular fractures risk avascular necrosis/non-union (often need arthroplasty); extracapsular fractures usually heal with fixation as the blood supply is preserved

cards.front: Posterior hip dislocation — limb posture and nerve at risk?
cards.back: Shortened, adducted and medially rotated limb; the sciatic nerve is at risk
A bimalleolar/trimalleolar fracture-dislocation of the ankle from forced eversion (the deltoid ligament avulses or the medial malleolus fractures)
Avulsion of the tuberosity (fibularis brevis pull) is common and heals well; a Jones fracture of the proximal shaft has a higher non-union risk
A stress fracture, classically of the 2nd metatarsal neck, after prolonged walking/marching
To localise the level of venous incompetence (saphenofemoral junction vs perforating veins)
Stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability; a calf DVT can embolise to the lungs

cards.front: Compartment syndrome of the leg — management?
cards.back: Urgent fasciotomy of all four compartments; do not wait for pulselessness, which is a late sign
The commonest peripheral arterial aneurysm; may thrombose or embolise and threaten the limb
Calf claudication suggests femoropopliteal disease; buttock/thigh claudication suggests aortoiliac disease (Leriche syndrome)
Normal ≈ 0.9–1.2; < 0.9 indicates peripheral arterial disease, and very low values suggest critical ischaemia
The 'gaiter' area above the medial malleolus, in a background of chronic venous insufficiency

cards.front: Great saphenous vein cutdown — why at the ankle?
cards.back: Its position is constant just anterior to the medial malleolus, giving reliable emergency venous access (mind the adjacent saphenous nerve)

cards.front: Unhappy triad of the knee — components?
cards.back: Torn ACL, medial collateral ligament and medial meniscus from a lateral blow to a planted leg
'Housemaid's knee', from prolonged kneeling; infrapatellar bursitis is 'clergyman's knee'
A popliteal synovial cyst, often communicating with the knee; rupture can mimic a calf DVT
Genu valgum = 'knock-knee' (legs angle inward); genu varum = 'bow-leg' (legs angle outward)
Inferior heel pain, worst with the first steps in the morning; tender at the medial calcaneal tuberosity

cards.cloze: The common fibular nerve is most often injured where it winds around the neck of the {{c1::fibula}}, causing foot drop.
The femoral nerve enters the thigh {{c1::lateral}} to the femoral artery, outside the femoral sheath.
The femoral head is supplied mainly by the {{c1::medial circumflex femoral}} artery.
The great saphenous vein passes {{c1::anterior}} to the medial malleolus — a constant landmark for a cutdown.
A positive {{c1::Trendelenburg}} sign indicates weakness of gluteus medius/minimus (superior gluteal nerve).
In the femoral triangle the order lateral to medial is nerve, artery, vein, canal — the mnemonic {{c1::NAVEL}}.
The femoral artery becomes the popliteal artery at the {{c1::adductor hiatus}}.
The tarsal tunnel lies behind the {{c1::medial malleolus}}, deep to the flexor retinaculum.
The ankle-jerk reflex tests the {{c1::S1}} root.
The most commonly sprained ankle ligament is the {{c1::anterior talofibular}} ligament (inversion injury).
A femoral hernia appears below and {{c1::lateral}} to the pubic tubercle.
The deepest neurovascular structure in the popliteal fossa is the {{c1::popliteal artery}}.
